claims.text: The target material is an as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi high-entropy alloy.
The as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi alloy has a single-phase hexagonal structure.
Deposition produces inherent lattice distortions and microstructural heterogeneity in the FeMnNiGeSi alloy.
Spatially varying lattice distortions and grain-boundary defects create a distribution of local magnetic exchange interactions.
The distribution of local exchange interactions governs the sharp, hysteretic magnetostructural transition.
The distribution of local exchange interactions governs the large magnetic entropy change.
Controlled annealing reduces microstructural heterogeneity in FeMnNiGeSi.
Annealing relieves internal stresses and makes the distribution of lattice distortions more uniform.
Microstructural homogenization narrows the distribution of local magnetostructural transition temperatures.
Narrowing the distribution of local transition temperatures produces a broader, less sharp macroscopic magnetocaloric transition.
Annealing reduces thermal hysteresis during low-field magnetic cycling.
Annealing slightly shifts or broadens the transition temperature relative to the as-deposited baseline.
After annealing, the entropy change remains significant but is moderated relative to the baseline.
The as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi baseline has a sharp, first-order magnetostructural transition with large hysteresis.
The as-deposited baseline has a limited heat-exchange rate because of a low surface-to-volume ratio.
The predicted mechanism applies only while the alloy remains single-phase and hexagonally ordered without precipitation or significant phase separation.
The prediction requires annealing to produce only moderate changes in grain size.
In the NiFeCoCrPdx alloy family, heat treatment and Pd additions reduce the distribution of exchange energies and produce a more magnetically homogeneous alloy.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says homogenization narrows the spread of local transition temperatures but then predicts a broader, less sharp macroscopic transition. Without an additional broadening mechanism, a narrower local-temperature distribution would ordinarily imply a sharper transition.
